title: Violin Sonata No. 5 in F major, “Spring”
hook: A violin sonata that opens with one of Beethoven’s sunniest tunes and hides a rhythmic practical joke in its scherzo.

painting.title: Springtime
painting.collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
painting.pairingNote: Two young people on a swing in a spring wood, light and carefree; the season the sonata was named after, though not by Beethoven.

facts: Beethoven finished the sonata in 1801, the year in which he first confided to friends, in letters, that he was losing his hearing. He meant it as the companion of the darker Sonata No. 4 in A minor; for reasons not known, the two were published separately, with different opus numbers. Both are dedicated to Count Moritz von Fries, a rich banker and patron, to whom Beethoven later dedicated the Seventh Symphony.
The nickname “Spring” is not Beethoven’s; it appeared after his death. It has stuck because the music is unusually warm and relaxed.
It is the first of his violin sonatas in four movements, with a short [[scherzo|scherzo]] added between the slow movement and the finale.
The title of the time was “sonata for piano and violin”, and the two are true partners: whoever has the tune, the other accompanies, and the roles keep changing.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a long, sunny tune and its dramatic shadow (I), a slow song without words (II), a one-minute rhythmic joke (III), and a gentle [[rondo|rondo]] that ends at a gallop (IV).

movements.heading: Allegro
movements.summary: The violin begins at once with a long, smiling melody over flowing piano figures; then the piano takes the melody and the violin accompanies. A more urgent second theme brings shadows and strong accents. The movement is a [[sonata-form|sonata form]], and Beethoven keeps passing his ideas back and forth between the two players.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a long, rising and falling melody, first in the violin.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: shorter, more insistent phrases with sharp accents, in a new key.

notice: Follow who has the tune. Almost every idea is heard twice, once in each instrument, and the accompaniment changes hands with it.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Gidon Kremer and Martha Argerich recorded all ten sonatas together for Deutsche Grammophon; this one was made in Berlin in March 1987. They take the exposition repeat.

movements.heading: Adagio molto espressivo
movements.summary: A slow song without words in B-flat major. The melody returns several times, more richly decorated each time, with the two instruments taking turns to sing it. Near the close, quiet repeated figures flutter like birdsong.

mainIdeas.name: The song
mainIdeas.description: a calm, long-breathed melody, first in the piano.

mainIdeas.name: The decorations
mainIdeas.description: on its returns, the melody is wrapped in quicker ornamental notes.

stops.hear: The piano alone begins a slow, singing melody
The violin takes up the melody; the piano adds soft, decorative figures
The mood darkens for a moment, in a minor key
The melody returns, ornamented with many small notes

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: Soft, fluttering repeated figures in both instruments, then a quiet close
stops.happening: The coda, often heard as birdsong

notice: Listen to how the melody is decorated each time it returns. The tune underneath stays the same.

movements.heading: Scherzo: Allegro molto
movements.summary: One of the shortest movements in all Beethoven’s sonatas, and a joke. The piano plays a short, bouncing phrase, and the violin plays the same phrase a beat behind, so that the two sound out of step. The middle section, the [[trio|trio]], is a quick run of scales.

mainIdeas.name: The scherzo
mainIdeas.description: a bouncing phrase, with the violin apparently one beat late.

mainIdeas.name: The trio
mainIdeas.description: fast scales running up and down in both instruments.

stops.hear: A short, bouncing phrase in the piano; the violin seems to come in a beat too late, and the two never quite line up
stops.happening: The scherzo and its rhythmic joke

stops.hear: Quick scales racing up and down
The bouncing phrase, still out of step

stops.label: Last 10 seconds
stops.hear: A short, light ending

notice: Tap along with the piano. When the violin enters, its accents fall exactly between yours. Schumann later borrowed the scherzo’s tune for the “Soldier’s March” in his *Album for the Young*.

movements.heading: Rondo: Allegro ma non troppo
movements.summary: A gentle, unhurried [[rondo|rondo]]: a friendly refrain that comes back between contrasting episodes. Once it returns in a surprising, distant key before finding its way home. Near the end the refrain becomes a lively galloping variation.

mainIdeas.name: The refrain
mainIdeas.description: a relaxed, lyrical tune, first in the piano, then the violin.

mainIdeas.name: The episodes
mainIdeas.description: livelier, sometimes stormier music between the refrains.

stops.hear: The piano plays a relaxed, friendly tune, and the violin repeats it

The friendly tune again
A stormier passage in a minor key, with strong accents
The refrain appears in an unexpected key, then slides gracefully back home
The tune is turned into a quick, galloping variation

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: A brisk, decisive close

notice: Listen for the moment around three minutes when the refrain begins in the “wrong” key. Beethoven lets it wander for a few bars before steering it home.

threads.title: Partners
threads.body: In all four movements the tune passes between violin and piano; neither is the accompanist for long.

threads.title: Light and shade
threads.body: Each sunny movement has its shadow: the urgent second theme, the minor-key passage of the Adagio, the stormy episode of the finale.

threads.title: Wit
threads.body: The scherzo’s out-of-step joke and the finale’s wrong-key return show the young Beethoven’s humour, as in the symphonies of the same years.
